claim: In offline reinforcement learning on pooled multi-robot data, updating the policy separately for fixed groups of robots chosen by morphological similarity makes the pooled policy better than updating on all robots at once and better than existing generic methods for resolving gradient conflicts between tasks, with the largest gains when most data are suboptimal. Supported only if it gives the highest mean return across all the expert, replay and mostly-suboptimal datasets; if on the mostly-suboptimal datasets it improves on plain pooled training by at least 20%; if grouping by morphology beats both random grouping and a coarse grouping by body type; and if its advantage survives giving the baseline the same number of optimiser steps and processed samples.

experiments: Build a pooled multi-robot locomotion benchmark with controlled data quality. Setup: 16 simulated robots in MuJoCo (nine quadrupeds, six bipeds, one hexapod), each trained with PPO to walk at a commanded 1 m/s forward or backward under a shared dense reward with robot-specific weights. For each robot and direction build three 1M-step datasets: expert rollouts of the converged policy, the whole training replay up to expert level (about 500M steps) subsampled uniformly, and a mix of 700k early, suboptimal steps with 300k late steps. A single network takes a shared observation part plus variable-length joint and foot sets aggregated by attention conditioned on morphology descriptors, extended with an action encoder for a Q-function. Each method uses about 100M sampled transitions per robot; report final return, mean +/- standard error over 5 seeds.

Check that morphological distance predicts which robots conflict. Setup: represent each robot as a graph of torso, joints and feet with node features for relative position and control parameters; compute pairwise Fused Gromov-Wasserstein distances, normalise to [0,1] and convert to similarity; correlate with mean pairwise gradient cosine across all robot pairs. Result: quadrupeds cluster together in both matrices, and similarity correlates with gradient alignment at Pearson r = 0.63 (p = 1.3e-14).

Compare morphology-grouped updates against plain pooling and generic conflict-resolution methods. Setup: cluster robots hierarchically on the morphological distance matrix into fixed groups, do one shared critic update per iteration and then one actor update per group in shuffled order; compare behaviour cloning, TD3+BC and implicit Q-learning, implicit Q-learning with gradient projection (PCGrad) and with dynamic affinity-based task grouping, and grouped versions of all three base learners, on all six datasets. Result: grouped implicit Q-learning has the highest mean (57.29 vs 52.05 plain, 55.07 affinity grouping, 53.48 PCGrad) and on the mostly-suboptimal data reaches 51.19 and 49.60 against 36.62 and 38.69; its average gain over plain pooling there is 33.99% against 18.33% and 7.15% for the two conflict-resolution methods. Grouping also lifts behaviour cloning by 26.3% and TD3+BC by 19.5% on those splits. It is not best everywhere: on expert-replay forward data grouped TD3+BC (57.04) and plain TD3+BC (55.66) beat it (54.62).

Rule out that any partition of the robots would help. Setup: on 70%-suboptimal forward data compare plain pooled implicit Q-learning, random grouping, a coarse four-way split by body type (bipeds, quadrupeds, hexapods, torso-less bipeds) and morphology-distance grouping. Result: 37.57 for plain pooling, 38.73 (+3.1%) for random groups, 34.45 (-8.3%) for the body-type split and 51.98 (+38.3%) for morphology-distance groups.

Rule out that the gain comes from taking more optimiser steps. Grouping performs one actor update per group per iteration, so the baseline gets fewer updates. Setup: give plain pooled implicit Q-learning M times as many optimiser steps with batches 1/M as large, so steps and processed samples both match, and compare on 70%-suboptimal forward data; separately sweep the number of groups M over {1, 2, 4, 7, 10, 13}. Result: the normalised baseline reaches 44.20 +/- 2.22 against 51.98 +/- 1.70 for grouping; performance peaks at moderate M (best at 7, with 2-4 already strong) and declines slightly with excessive partitioning, while wall-clock time grows with M.
